---
title: "Signal-Based Review: A Methodology for AI-Integrated Assessment"
---

## Overview

Signal-based review is an assessment methodology in which computational tools analyse student work to surface patterns, anomalies, and indicators that inform -- but do not replace -- human evaluative judgment. The assessor receives a structured set of signals derived from that analysis, interprets them in context, and makes all consequential decisions: whether to investigate further, how to weight the evidence, and ultimately what mark and feedback to assign.

The methodology is tool-agnostic. Signals may be generated by machine learning models, natural language processing pipelines, static code analysis, computer vision techniques, or simpler rule-based scripts. What defines signal-based review is not the instrument but the role it plays: signals are inputs to human judgment, never substitutes for it.

---

## The Core Distinction: Signals vs Verdicts

The defining principle of signal-based review is the distinction between a **signal** and a **verdict**.

A verdict is a conclusion: "this work merits a grade of 65." A signal is an observation: "the vocabulary distribution in this submission is atypical relative to the student's prior work." Signals are hypothesis-generating. They prompt the assessor to look more carefully, ask a question, or investigate a specific aspect of the work. They carry no evaluative weight on their own.

This distinction is not merely semantic. It reflects a deliberate allocation of cognitive and professional responsibility. Computational tools are well-suited to pattern detection at scale: they are consistent, tireless, and indifferent to social cues. Human assessors are well-suited to interpretation in context: they understand discipline norms, can weigh competing considerations, and bear professional and ethical accountability for their judgments. Signal-based review assigns each role accordingly.

---

## Workflow

The signal-based review process follows four stages:

### 1. Submission

Student work is received in its native format: source code repositories, written documents, video recordings, presentations, or structured data files. No special submission format is required beyond what the assessment task already specifies.

### 2. Signal Generation

Analytical tools process the submission and produce a signal report. Depending on the submission type, signals may include:

**For written work:** vocabulary range and consistency, sentence-level complexity patterns, structural coherence indicators, lexical similarity to reference corpora, anomalies in register or voice across sections.

**For code:** cyclomatic complexity, adherence to style conventions, test coverage, dependency patterns, commit history characteristics, similarity to known repositories or solutions.

**For video:** speech rate and fluency patterns, slide transition timing, gaze and gesture indicators (where ethically permissible), audio quality markers.

The signal report is a structured document or dashboard, not a grade. It presents observations with associated confidence levels and flags areas that warrant closer attention.

### 3. Assessor Interpretation

The assessor reviews the submission alongside the signal report. Signals function as prompts: they direct attention, raise questions, and occasionally prompt direct follow-up with the student (for example, a clarifying discussion or additional task). The assessor is not required to act on any signal, and may disregard signals they judge to be artefacts, irrelevant, or misleading in context.

The locus of judgment remains entirely with the assessor. The signal report is one input among many, alongside the work itself, the marking rubric, knowledge of the student's context, and professional experience.

### 4. Mark and Feedback Assignment

The assessor assigns the mark and writes or approves feedback based on their holistic reading of the submission. The signal report may have contributed to that reading, or it may not. Either way, the mark and feedback are the assessor's professional output, not a downstream product of the computational analysis.

---

## Philosophy

### The Human-in-the-Loop Imperative

Signal-based review is designed around the principle that consequential decisions about students must remain with qualified humans. This is not a constraint reluctantly accepted for political reasons; it is a positive methodological commitment. Students have a right to be assessed by someone who understands their context, can exercise discretion, and is accountable for the outcome. Automated systems cannot fulfil that obligation.

At the same time, the volume and complexity of modern assessment creates genuine risk of inconsistency, fatigue-induced error, and missed patterns. Tools that can surface relevant signals without exercising judgment offer a way to address these risks without displacing human responsibility.

### The Tool-Methodology Distinction

It is tempting to name the tools used in assessment workflows, particularly when those tools are novel or topical. This is generally unhelpful. Methodology is defined by what is done, not by what instrument is used to do it. A physician who uses a stethoscope and one who uses an ultrasound are both "listening to the heart"; the instrument is incidental to the diagnostic act.

Signal-based review is a methodology. The tools that generate signals are implementation details. Describing the methodology in terms of its tools introduces several problems: it dates quickly as the technical landscape changes, it invites debate about the specific tools rather than the underlying approach, and it obscures the methodological logic that makes the approach defensible.

This has practical consequences for how the methodology is described in assessment policies, unit outlines, and research publications. Referring to "signal-based review" rather than "AI-assisted marking" or "machine learning analysis" produces documentation that remains accurate and readable across the lifecycle of the methodology, regardless of which tools are in use at any given time.

### Analogy to Established Practice

Signal-based review sits within a long tradition of tool-assisted professional judgment. Pathologists use algorithmic screening to flag regions of interest in tissue samples; the diagnosis is the pathologist's. Financial auditors use automated anomaly detection to prioritise their investigations; the audit opinion is the auditor's. Plagiarism detection systems flag textual similarity; the academic misconduct determination is the examiner's.

In each case, the tool performs a detection function; the professional performs an interpretive and consequential function. Signal-based review applies the same architecture to assessment.

### Consistency and Equity

One underappreciated benefit of signal-based review is the potential for greater consistency and equity across a cohort. Human assessors are subject to fatigue, implicit bias, and the anchoring effects of earlier submissions. Computational signals are consistent: the same signal generation process applied to two submissions produces comparable outputs regardless of the order in which they are processed, the time of day, or the assessor's prior workload.

Signals do not eliminate assessor variability, but they can provide a consistent reference point that supports more structured and defensible decision-making, particularly in large cohorts or multi-assessor marking teams.

---

## Relationship to Assessment Integrity

Signal-based review is not primarily an integrity tool, though signals related to academic integrity may be among those generated. The methodology is designed to support richer, more informed feedback and more consistent marking, with integrity signals as one component among many.

This framing matters. Assessment processes oriented primarily around detection create adversarial dynamics that undermine the pedagogical relationship. Signal-based review is oriented around understanding student work more deeply, with the assessor remaining in control of how that understanding is used.

---

## Transparency and Student Communication

Students should be informed that their work may be analysed using computational tools as part of the assessment process, in the same way they are informed of other assessment practices. This disclosure is consistent with institutional obligations around data handling and assessment transparency.

The framing for students is straightforward: analytical tools help the assessor look more carefully at submitted work; the assessor makes all decisions about marks and feedback. This is an accurate description, and most students find it unremarkable, particularly when it is associated with more specific and timely feedback.

---

## Limitations and Ongoing Considerations

Signal-based review is not a panacea. Signals can be misleading: a student whose writing style changed dramatically between submissions may generate anomaly signals for entirely legitimate reasons. Tools trained on particular populations or text types may produce biased signals when applied to students whose work falls outside those distributions.

These limitations reinforce, rather than undermine, the case for keeping the assessor in the loop. A methodology that depends on human interpretation is resilient to tool-level errors in a way that automated marking is not. The assessor who understands what a signal is and is not will recognise when a signal warrants investigation and when it should be set aside.

Ongoing attention to signal validity, tool bias, and assessor calibration is part of responsible implementation of this methodology.

---

*This document describes a general methodology applicable across assessment contexts. Specific implementations will vary by discipline, submission type, and institutional context.*
